title: Greatly Beloved
subtitle: Daniel in Poems & Pictures
author: Timothy Holt
beforeYouBegin:
Daniel begins with temple cups packed off to Babylon and a young man asking for vegetables and water. Then come a king's forgotten dream, a statue with feet of clay, a stone cut without hands, three friends who say "but if not, " a fourth man walking in the fire, a hand writing on a lamp-lit wall, and an open window toward Jerusalem on the night before the lions. The last chapters turn to visions by great rivers, and end with the wise shining like the stars.

This book walks through it in forty short poems, in five parts. Each poem sits beside a picture and under a single line of Scripture. The pictures stay with the things the story touches—a plain bowl, a furnace glow, a plaster wall, lions asleep in the morning light— and the visions are shown only as sea, cloud, river, and light.

The poems are not the Bible. They are one reader's response to it. Open the book of Daniel alongside this book, and let the real words have the last word.

parts.title: The King's Table
parts.epigraph: But Daniel purposed in his heart that he would not defile himself
parts.lightHint: Near 'the cups' (Daniel 1:1–2) in Part 1: The King's Table

parts.title: The Statue and the Furnace
parts.epigraph: His kingdom is an everlasting kingdom. His dominion is from generation to generation.
parts.lightName: Light of The Statue and the Furnace
parts.lightHint: Near 'feet of clay' (Daniel 2:31–33) in Part 2: The Statue and the Furnace

parts.title: The Writing and the Lions
parts.epigraph: for he is the living God, and steadfast forever.
parts.lightName: Light of The Writing and the Lions
parts.lightHint: Near 'the cups again' (Daniel 5:2–4) in Part 3: The Writing and the Lions

parts.title: Visions in the Night
parts.epigraph: But the saints of the Most High will receive the kingdom, and possess the kingdom forever, even forever and ever.
parts.lightName: Light of Visions in the Night
parts.lightHint: Near 'the great sea' (Daniel 7:1–3) in Part 4: Visions in the Night

parts.title: Until the End
parts.epigraph: At that time your people will be delivered, everyone who is found written in the book.
parts.lightHint: Near 'plain bread' (Daniel 10:2–3) in Part 5: Until the End

paintings.title: the cups
paintings.epigraph: “The Lord gave Jehoiakim king of Judah into his hand, with part of the vessels of the house of God”
paintings.poem:
they took the cups first—
bowls from the temple,
wrapped in straw,
carried off
to a stranger's treasure house.

then they took the young men.

the story opens
with every holy thing
in the wrong place.

but read the line again:
the Lord gave them.

even carried away,
they were never
out of his hands.
paintings.reflectionPrompt: Every stop on the Pilgrim Walk shows how God meets us in ordinary places (Daniel 1:1–2)—where in your own home or work today does “even carried away, they were never out of his hands” ring true?

paintings.title: new names
paintings.epigraph: “to Daniel he gave the name Belteshazzar”
paintings.poem:
the official wrote down
new names
for four young men—
Belteshazzar,
Shadrach, Meshach,
Abednego—
names that belonged
to someone else's gods.

you can rename a boy.
you can teach him
a new language
and three years
of Chaldean books.

but a name
is only what they call you.

it was never
what God called them.
paintings.reflectionPrompt: Take a slow breath and read the final line again: “it was never what God called them.” How would you walk through the next hour differently if you carried that truth with you?

paintings.title: a different plate
paintings.epigraph: “Therefore he requested of the prince of the eunuchs that he might not defile himself.”
paintings.poem:
it was only dinner.
the best in the empire,
sent from the king's own table.

no one would have blamed him.
far from home,
no temple, no family,
a young man doing
what he was told.

but somewhere in him
there was a line,
and he knew where it was.

he didn't make a scene.
he asked,
politely,
for a different plate.

that's the quiet kind of courage:
deciding who you are
before the platter comes.12
paintings.reflectionPrompt: Think of a season when you knew the feeling of “it was only dinner.” Looking through the lens of Daniel 1:8, what does it mean to discover that “that's the quiet kind of courage: deciding who you are before the platter comes.12”?

paintings.title: ten days
paintings.epigraph: “let them give us vegetables to eat, and water to drink.”
paintings.poem:
test us,
he said.
ten days.

a bowl of greens.
a cup of water.

and the steward
said yes.

on the tenth day
they looked better
and stronger
than all the rest.

not because vegetables are magic.

because God
honors a small faithfulness
kept at a plain table
where no one is watching
but him.
paintings.reflectionPrompt: Look closely at the table set before you in this painting (Daniel 1:12–15)—if you could leave one anxious weight beside it today, what would you set down?

paintings.title: the books of Babylon
paintings.epigraph: “God gave them knowledge and skill in all learning and wisdom”
paintings.poem:
they learned the books of Babylon,
the tablets,
the language,
the whole library of a foreign court.

they didn't refuse to learn.
they refused to bow.

and God
gave them more
than their teachers had.

you can study everything
in a strange land

and keep your heart
pointed home.
paintings.reflectionPrompt: Let your eyes rest on the brushwork and light around the quiet centerpiece of “the books of Babylon”: what quiet prayer rises in you when you read, “you can study everything in a strange land and keep your heart pointed home”?

paintings.title: four around a lamp
paintings.epigraph: “that they would desire mercies of the God of heaven concerning this secret”
paintings.poem:
the king wanted a dream
no one could know.
the order was out:
all the wise men would die.

and Daniel
did the wisest thing
a wise man can do.

he went home
and told his friends.

four young men
around one small lamp,
asking heaven for mercy.

not a strategy.
not a backup plan.

just friends
who knew how to pray,
and a God
who knew the dream.
paintings.reflectionPrompt: Linger with the movement in “four around a lamp” (Daniel 2:17–18) from “the king wanted a dream no one could know” to “just friends who knew how to pray, and a God who knew the dream”—where do you find yourself along that arc today?

paintings.title: the light lives with him
paintings.epigraph: “He knows what is in the darkness, and the light dwells with him.”
paintings.poem:
the secret came
in the night.

and before he ran to the king,
before he saved his own life,
Daniel stopped
and blessed God.

he changes the times.
he knows what hides in the dark.

it isn't that the dark
is empty.

it's that nothing in it
is hidden from him—

and the light
has always
lived with him.
paintings.reflectionPrompt: Notice how “the light lives with him” (Daniel 2:19–22) arrives at: “it's that nothing in it is hidden from him— and the light has always lived with him.” Who in your life is walking a hard stretch of road today and needs you to share this grace with them?

paintings.title: not me
paintings.epigraph: “this secret is not revealed to me for any wisdom that I have more than any living”
paintings.poem:
he could have taken the credit.
the whole court was waiting.
the king's eyes were on him.

instead he said:
it isn't me.

there is a God in heaven
who reveals secrets.

the first thing Daniel told the king
wasn't the dream.

it was who gave it.
paintings.reflectionPrompt: What if the most important thing you remember before tonight is the quiet lesson of Daniel 2:27–30: “the first thing Daniel told the king wasn't the dream. it was who gave it”?

paintings.title: feet of clay
paintings.epigraph: “its feet part of iron, and part of clay.”
paintings.poem:
gold at the head,
then silver,
bronze,
iron—
each metal harder,
each one worth less.

and at the bottom,
holding the whole bright thing up,
feet of iron
mixed with clay.

every empire
looks like gold
from the top.

look lower.
paintings.reflectionPrompt: Imagine standing inside this frame beside the quiet centerpiece of “feet of clay”: what hurry or noise in your week begins to fade when you hear, “every empire looks like gold from the top. look lower”?

paintings.title: a stone cut without hands
paintings.epigraph: “a stone was cut out without hands”
paintings.poem:
no quarry.
no chisel.
no king's name
carved on its side.

just a stone
no one made,

striking the statue
at its weakest place.

gold, silver, bronze, iron, clay—
blown away like chaff
from a summer threshing floor.

and the stone
kept growing
until it was a mountain
and filled the whole earth.

that's how his kingdom comes:
not built by us.
not stopped by anyone.
paintings.reflectionPrompt: Read the closing words aloud in the stillness: “and the stone kept growing until it was a mountain and filled the whole earth. not stopped by anyone.” What part of your heart feels most searched or comforted by Daniel 2:34–35 right now?

paintings.title: never destroyed
paintings.epigraph: “the God of heaven will set up a kingdom which will never be destroyed”
paintings.poem:
Babylon is dust now.
so are the palaces
of every king
who came after.

you can walk
where the walls stood
and not know it.

but in the days of those kings
another kingdom began—
quietly,
without a capital
you could point to.

it has never been
handed to anyone else.

it is still standing,
and the door
is still open.
paintings.reflectionPrompt: In Daniel 2:44, grace meets us right beside the stones of the wall: how does the closing thought—“it is still standing, and the door is still open”—steady your footing for the road ahead?

paintings.title: able
paintings.epigraph: “our God whom we serve is able to deliver us from the burning fiery furnace”
paintings.poem:
the music started,
and a whole plain
went down on its knees.

horn, flute, lyre, harp—
everyone bowing
to sixty cubits of gold.

three young men
stayed standing.

not proud.
not loud.

they told the king:
we don't need to argue this.

our God is able.

that was the whole speech.
paintings.reflectionPrompt: If today’s painting of “able” (Daniel 3:16–17) hung beside the door you walk out of this morning, how would its final line—“that was the whole speech”—shape your choices?

paintings.title: but if not
paintings.epigraph: “But if not, let it be known to you, O king, that we will not serve your gods”
paintings.poem:
he is able.
he will deliver us.

and then the three words
that hold up everything:

but if not.

their faith
didn't depend
on how the story ended.

they didn't know
about the fourth man yet.
they only knew
whom they served.

this is love
that doesn't ask
for a guarantee.
paintings.reflectionPrompt: Every stop on the Pilgrim Walk shows how God meets us in ordinary places (Daniel 3:18)—where in your own home or work today does “this is love that doesn't ask for a guarantee” ring true?

paintings.title: a fourth in the fire
paintings.epigraph: “Look, I see four men loose, walking in the middle of the fire, and they are unharmed.”
paintings.poem:
three went in bound.

the king leaned forward
and counted
four.

loose.
unharmed.
not running—
walking,
as if it were a garden.

they did not get
out of the fire.

they got company
in it.

sometimes that's the rescue:
not a door that keeps you out,
but someone
who walks in beside you.
paintings.reflectionPrompt: Take a slow breath and read the final line again: “sometimes that's the rescue: not a door that keeps you out, but someone who walks in beside you.” How would you walk through the next hour differently if you carried that truth with you?

paintings.title: not even the smell
paintings.epigraph: “the smell of fire wasn’t even on them.”
paintings.poem:
only the ropes
were gone.

not a hair singed.
not a hem changed.
not even the smell of smoke
on their clothes.

some trouble you walk out of
still carrying—
the smell of it
on everything.

this time
God took it all.

may he do that for you:
bring you through,
and bring you out
clean.
paintings.reflectionPrompt: Think of a season when you knew the feeling of “only the ropes were gone.” Looking through the lens of Daniel 3:26–27, what does it mean to discover that “may he do that for you: bring you through, and bring you out clean”?

paintings.title: the stump
paintings.epigraph: “Nevertheless leave the stump of its roots in the earth”
paintings.poem:
a tree that touched the sky,
birds in every branch,
fruit enough for all.

and a voice from heaven:
cut it down.

but—
leave the stump.
leave the roots.
let the dew fall on it.

even the judgment
had a mercy
folded inside it.

God brought the king down
and left something
to grow back.
paintings.reflectionPrompt: Look closely at the deep roots of the tree in this painting (Daniel 4:14–15)—if you could leave one anxious weight beside it today, what would you set down?

paintings.title: looking up
paintings.epigraph: “my understanding returned to me”
paintings.poem:
is not this great Babylon,
which I have built?

he said it in his palace
and lost it all
while the words
were still in his mouth.

seven times passed over him
in the wet grass.
then one day he looked up.

he lifted his eyes,
his mind came back,
and the first thing he did
was praise.

pride looks down
at what it built.

healing
looks up.
paintings.reflectionPrompt: Let your eyes rest on the brushwork and light around the quiet centerpiece of “looking up”: what quiet prayer rises in you when you read, “pride looks down at what it built. healing looks up”?

paintings.title: the cups again
paintings.epigraph: “the golden and silver vessels which Nebuchadnezzar his father had taken out of the temple”
paintings.poem:
remember the cups
from the first page?

years later
someone brought them out
of the treasure house
for a party.

holy things
passed down the table,
filled with wine,
raised to gods
of wood and stone.

Belshazzar thought
they were only cups.

he thought
no one was keeping count.
paintings.reflectionPrompt: Linger with the movement in “the cups again” (Daniel 5:2–4) from “remember the cups from the first page?” to “he thought no one was keeping count”—where do you find yourself along that arc today?

paintings.title: the plaster wall
paintings.epigraph: “the fingers of a man’s hand came out and wrote near the lamp stand on the plaster of the wall”
paintings.poem:
in the same hour,
while the wine was still going round,

near the lamp stand,
where the light was brightest,
fingers were writing
on the plaster.

no body.
no voice.
just a hand,
and a message.

the king's knees
knocked together.

all the wise men of Babylon
came in and stared,

and not one of them
could read it.
paintings.reflectionPrompt: Notice how “the plaster wall” (Daniel 5:5–8) arrives at: “all the wise men of Babylon came in and stared, and not one of them could read it.” Who in your life is walking a hard stretch of road today and needs you to share this grace with them?

paintings.title: keep your gifts
paintings.epigraph: “Let your gifts be to yourself, and give your rewards to another.”
paintings.poem:
purple robes.
a chain of gold.
the third seat in the kingdom.

Daniel said:
keep them.
I'll read it anyway.

he couldn't be bought
because he wasn't selling.

the truth
was never his
to put a price on.
paintings.reflectionPrompt: What if the most important thing you remember before tonight is the quiet lesson of Daniel 5:16–17: “the truth was never his to put a price on”?

paintings.title: your breath
paintings.epigraph: “the God in whose hand your breath is, and whose are all your ways”
paintings.poem:
you praised gods of silver and gold,
Daniel told the king,
of bronze and iron,
of wood and stone—

gods that don't see,
don't hear,
don't know.

and the God
who holds your breath
in his hand
you never thanked.

it's a hard word.
but read it again, gently:

every breath you've taken
today
was held
by someone.
paintings.reflectionPrompt: Imagine standing inside this frame beside the quiet rhythm of your breath: what hurry or noise in your week begins to fade when you hear, “but read it again, gently: every breath you've taken today was held by someone”?

paintings.title: weighed
paintings.epigraph: “you are weighed in the balances, and are found wanting.”
paintings.poem:
counted.
weighed.
divided.

three words on a wall,
and that same night
the kingdom passed
to someone else.

it's frightening
to be weighed.

every one of us
would come up light.

that's why the good news
was never
that we are heavy enough.

it's that mercy
has a thumb
on the scale.
paintings.reflectionPrompt: Read the closing words aloud in the stillness: “it's that mercy has a thumb on the scale.” What part of your heart feels most searched or comforted by Daniel 5:26–28 right now?

paintings.title: no fault
paintings.epigraph: “they could find no occasion or fault, because he was faithful.”
paintings.poem:
they went through
every ledger,
every account,
every decision
he had ever signed.

they were looking
for one mistake.

they found none.

so they went looking
at his prayers instead.

imagine a life
so honest
the only charge against you
is that you love God.
paintings.reflectionPrompt: In Daniel 6:4–5, grace meets us right beside the quiet centerpiece of “no fault”: how does the closing thought—“imagine a life so honest the only charge against you is that you love God”—steady your footing for the road ahead?

paintings.title: windows open toward Jerusalem
paintings.epigraph: “now his windows were open in his room toward Jerusalem”
paintings.poem:
he knew the law was signed.
he knew who was watching.

he went upstairs anyway,
to the windows open
toward a city
he hadn't seen
since he was young,

and knelt,
three times a day,
and gave thanks,
as he did before.

not in defiance.
in habit.

he didn't start praying
because of the lions.

he had been praying
all along.
paintings.reflectionPrompt: If today’s painting of “windows open toward Jerusalem” (Daniel 6:10) hung beside the door you walk out of this morning, how would its final line—“he had been praying all along”—shape your choices?

paintings.title: the king's long night
paintings.epigraph: “his sleep fled from him.”
paintings.poem:
the one who signed the law
couldn't sleep.

no music. no supper.
a whole night with a decree
he couldn't take back.

very early he ran
to the sealed stone
and called into the dark,
his voice shaking:

is your God
able?

it's the same question
another king asked
at the furnace.

the answer
hasn't changed.
paintings.reflectionPrompt: Every stop on the Pilgrim Walk shows how God meets us in ordinary places (Daniel 6:18–20)—where in your own home or work today does “the answer hasn't changed” ring true?

paintings.title: the lions' den
paintings.epigraph: “My God has sent his angel, and has shut the lions’ mouths”
paintings.poem:
all night
in the dark
with lions.

no one saw
what happened down there.
only the morning,
and a voice from below:

O king, live forever.

no harm was found on him,
the book says,
because he had trusted
in his God.

and the lions,
it seems,
slept better
than the king did.
paintings.reflectionPrompt: Take a slow breath and read the final line again: “and the lions, it seems, slept better than the king did.” How would you walk through the next hour differently if you carried that truth with you?

paintings.title: the great sea
paintings.epigraph: “the four winds of the sky broke out on the great sea.”
paintings.poem:
in the first year of Belshazzar—
before the wall,
before the lions—
Daniel dreamed
of the sea.

the four winds broke on it,
and out of the deep
came terrible things,
one after another.

that's how the world can feel:
wind from every side,
the water never still.

he wrote it down.
he told the sum of it.

and he kept watching,
because the vision
wasn't finished yet.
paintings.reflectionPrompt: Think of a season when you knew the feeling of “in the first year of Belshazzar— before the wall, before the lions— Daniel dreamed of the sea.” Looking through the lens of Daniel 7:1–3, what does it mean to discover that “and he kept watching, because the vision wasn't finished yet”?

paintings.title: ancient of days
paintings.epigraph: “one who was ancient of days sat. His clothing was white as snow”
paintings.poem:
thrones were set,
and one sat down
who was older than every empire—

clothing white as snow,
hair like pure wool,
a stream of fire
flowing out before him.

the books were opened.

after all that roaring,
this:
someone sitting down.

not hurried.
not afraid.

the judge has taken his seat,
and the sea
has nothing more to say.
paintings.reflectionPrompt: Look closely at the stream bank in this painting (Daniel 7:9–10)—if you could leave one anxious weight beside it today, what would you set down?

paintings.title: one like a son of man
paintings.epigraph: “there came with the clouds of the sky one like a son of man”
paintings.poem:
the kingdoms of the world
came up from the sea.

this one came
with the clouds.

one like a son of man,
brought near
to the ancient of days,

and given a kingdom
that will not pass away.

long after,
standing before the high priest,
Jesus would answer
with these very words:

the Son of Man,
coming with the clouds.
paintings.reflectionPrompt: Let your eyes rest on the brushwork and light around the guiding cloud: what quiet prayer rises in you when you read, “long after, standing before the high priest, Jesus would answer with these very words: the Son of Man, coming with the clouds”?

paintings.title: kept
paintings.epigraph: “my thoughts much troubled me, and my face was changed in me; but I kept the matter in my heart.”
paintings.poem:
he saw it.
he didn't understand all of it.
it troubled him.

and he didn't
throw it away.

he didn't explain it away,
either.

he kept it,
the way you keep
a letter you can't read yet—

close,
turning it over,
trusting
the one who wrote it.
paintings.reflectionPrompt: Linger with the movement in “kept” (Daniel 7:28) from “he saw it. he didn't understand all of it” to “he kept it, the way you keep a letter you can't read yet— close, turning it over, trusting the one who wrote it”—where do you find yourself along that arc today?

paintings.title: Gabriel
paintings.epigraph: “Gabriel, make this man understand the vision.”
paintings.poem:
by the river Ulai
a voice called across the water:
Gabriel,
make this man understand.

and heaven
sent a teacher.

Daniel fell on his face.
he fell into a deep sleep.

and the angel
touched him
and set him upright.

that's still how it goes.
the truth doesn't come
to crush you.

it comes
to stand you up.
paintings.reflectionPrompt: Notice how “Gabriel” (Daniel 8:15–18) arrives at: “that's still how it goes. it comes to stand you up.” Who in your life is walking a hard stretch of road today and needs you to share this grace with them?

paintings.title: seventy years
paintings.epigraph: “I, Daniel, understood by the books the number of the years”
paintings.poem:
he found it in Jeremiah:
seventy years.

and Daniel,
who had lived through
most of them,
counted.

a promise
with a number on it.

he didn't just wait for it.
he prayed toward it—
with fasting,
with sackcloth and ashes.

reading the promise
didn't make him pray less.

it made him
pray more.
paintings.reflectionPrompt: What if the most important thing you remember before tonight is the quiet lesson of Daniel 9:2–3: “he prayed toward it— with fasting, with sackcloth and ashes. it made him pray more”?

paintings.title: Lord, hear
paintings.epigraph: “Lord, hear. Lord, forgive. Lord, listen and do.”
paintings.poem:
we have sinned,
he prayed.

we.
not they.

the one man in Babylon
they could find no fault in
stood in line
with everyone else.

he didn't ask
because they deserved it.
he asked
because God is merciful.

hear. forgive. listen and do.

that's the whole prayer
of anyone
who has ever come home.
paintings.reflectionPrompt: Imagine standing inside this frame beside the quiet centerpiece of “Lord, hear”: what hurry or noise in your week begins to fade when you hear, “that's the whole prayer of anyone who has ever come home”?

paintings.title: the evening hour
paintings.epigraph: “for you are greatly beloved.”
paintings.poem:
he had spent the whole prayer
telling God
what his people were:
wayward,
ashamed,
far from home.

Gabriel came swiftly,
about the time of the evening offering,
and told Daniel
what he was:

greatly beloved.

you bring God
the truth about yourself.

he answers
with the truth
about you.
paintings.reflectionPrompt: Read the closing words aloud in the stillness: “he answers with the truth about you.” What part of your heart feels most searched or comforted by Daniel 9:21–23 right now?

paintings.title: plain bread
paintings.epigraph: “I ate no pleasant bread. No meat or wine came into my mouth.”
paintings.poem:
three whole weeks
of mourning.

plain bread.
no meat,
no wine,
no oil for his skin.

the young man who once asked
for vegetables and water
was still at the same table,
still choosing
the plainer plate.

some things
you learn young
and keep.
paintings.reflectionPrompt: In Daniel 10:2–3, grace meets us right beside the table set before you: how does the closing thought—“some things you learn young and keep”—steady your footing for the road ahead?

paintings.title: twenty-one days
paintings.epigraph: “from the first day that you set your heart to understand”
paintings.poem:
three weeks of fasting,
and nothing.

then, by the great river,
a hand set him on his knees:

your words were heard
from the first day.

the answer had been sent.
it met resistance
we cannot see—
twenty-one days of it.

so when heaven seems quiet,
it may not be
that no one heard.

it may be
that someone is still
on the way.
paintings.reflectionPrompt: If today’s painting of “twenty-one days” (Daniel 10:10–13) hung beside the door you walk out of this morning, how would its final line—“it may be that someone is still on the way”—shape your choices?

paintings.title: o man greatly beloved
paintings.epigraph: “Greatly beloved man, don’t be afraid. Peace be to you. Be strong. Y es, be strong.”
paintings.poem:
no strength left.
no breath left.
he couldn't even speak.

so heaven touched his lips,
and then touched him again,

and said the gentlest thing
in the whole book:

don't be afraid.
peace.
be strong—
yes, be strong.

he said it twice,
as if he knew
once
would not be enough.

greatly beloved—
that's what he calls you, too,
when you have nothing left.
paintings.reflectionPrompt: Every stop on the Pilgrim Walk shows how God meets us in ordinary places (Daniel 10:16–19)—where in your own home or work today does “greatly beloved— that's what he calls you, too, when you have nothing left” ring true?

paintings.title: the people who know their God
paintings.epigraph: “the people who know their God will be strong, and take action.”
paintings.poem:
chapter eleven is a long march of kings,
north and south,
armies coming and going.

but in the middle of all that noise,
one quiet line:

the people who know their God
will be strong.

not the loudest.
the ones who know him.

and when some of them fall,
even that is to refine them,
like silver,
and make them white.
paintings.reflectionPrompt: Take a slow breath and read the final line again: “and when some of them fall, even that is to refine them, like silver, and make them white.” How would you walk through the next hour differently if you carried that truth with you?

paintings.title: like the stars
paintings.epigraph: “Those who are wise will shine as the brightness of the expanse.”
paintings.poem:
many who sleep in the dust
will wake.

and the wise
will shine like the sky,
and those who turn many
toward what is right,
like the stars,
forever.

not the kings from chapter eleven.
not the statue.
not the empires.

the ones who taught a neighbor,
kept a promise,
kept praying—

they're the ones
who will still be shining
when every palace
is dust.92
paintings.reflectionPrompt: Think of a season when you knew the feeling of “many who sleep in the dust will wake.” Looking through the lens of Daniel 12:2–3, what does it mean to discover that “the ones who taught a neighbor, kept a promise, kept praying— they're the ones who will still be shining when every palace is dust.92”?

paintings.title: go your way
paintings.epigraph: “But go your way until the end; for you will rest”
paintings.poem:
how long?
what will the end be?

he had read the dreams
of kings.
and at the very end he said:
I heard,
but I didn't understand.

the answer wasn't a map.
it was a blessing:

go your way. you will rest.
you will stand in your inheritance.

you don't have to know
how it ends.

just go your way,
the way you always have—

windows open,
toward home.
paintings.reflectionPrompt: Look closely at the open window facing home in this painting (Daniel 12:8–13)—if you could leave one anxious weight beside it today, what would you set down?
